source.version: Working paper dated March 2, 2026 (title page), from coauthor Artem Timoshenko's website; newer than the 2025 SSRN posting (SSRN 5371575). Main text 43 PDF pages plus a 25-page Web Appendix (WA-1 to WA-25) dated March 2, 2026.
source.title_on_document: Guided Creativity: AI Intermediation for Enhancing Originality and Quality in Visual Design

supplement.where: Web Appendix appended to the same PDF (PDF pp. 45-69, numbered WA-1 to WA-25)
supplement.holds: Full regression tables with designer-clustered standard errors: Table WA-C.1 (quality, mean and quantile), WA-C.2 (embedding originality under four high-quality definitions), WA-C.3 and WA-C.4 (contrasts with SEs) for Study 1; Tables WA-D.1 to WA-D.5 and Figure WA-D.2 for the restaurant replication; pipeline validation studies (WA-B.3). Nothing needed for extraction appears to sit outside this PDF.

paper_design_summary: Professional freelance designers who registered for a real logo design contest on freelancer.com were randomly assigned to galleries: no exemplars (Blind), 60 rated human-made exemplars (Open), or AI-generated variations of those exemplars (one per exemplar, Variation(1); four per exemplar, Variation(4)), made by the authors' fine-tuned FLUX.1-dev pipeline. Submitted logos were scored for quality (survey-based click attractiveness) and originality (minimum CLIP cosine distance to the 12 top exemplars, plus a perception-based survey measure). A second contest for a restaurant brand replicated the design with Open, Blind, and Variation(4) arms.

studies.label: Field experiment 1: healthcare brand logo contest (Armor Health)

participants.exclusions: 440 designers registered (were randomized upon registration); 292 submitted at least one logo and form the analysis sample (148 registered designers submitted nothing: Open 35, Variation(1) 34, Variation(4) 44, Blind 35). Registration did not require participation. Quality regressions use all 2,199 submissions of the 292 designers; embedding-originality regressions use only the top 50 submissions by quality in each condition (200 observations), and the paper does not say how many designers those submissions come from.
participants.who: Professional freelance logo designers recruited on freelancer.com; average of over 25 completed projects
participants.quote: A total of 440 designers registered for the experiment, with 292 designers submitting at least one logo (Table 1).
participants.locator: PDF p. 20 (printed p. 19), text and Table 1

ai_tool.name_model: Authors' custom pipeline: JoyCaption image captioning to produce structured text descriptions of each exemplar, then FLUX.1-dev text-to-image fine-tuned with two LoRAs (Logo LoRA trained on about 25,000 restaurant-contest logos; Optimization LoRA trained on 50 survey-rated logo pairs)
ai_tool.how_used: Designers did not interact with the model. The researchers generated variations of the 60 exemplars in advance and displayed them in a gallery (5 pages, 12 per page, ranked by the originals' ratings) that assigned designers could view during the two-week contest.

task.description: Create a new logo for a small healthcare brand (Armor Health) in a crowdsourcing contest with a $400 prize; designers were told the goal was logos that attract clicks in online display ads. Designers could submit several logos (2,199 in total); 10 random new submissions per condition received private ratings each day.

outcomes.name: Embedding-based originality of high-quality submissions
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Minimum cosine distance between a submission's CLIP embedding (CLIP-ViT-bigG-14-laion2B) and the 12 leading exemplars on the first gallery page. Main sample: top 50 submissions by click attractiveness in each condition. Robustness variants in Table WA-C.2/C.4: top 100 per condition, top 200 and top 400 across all submissions. OLS at submission level with condition indicators, submission day, designer-level controls; SEs clustered by designer. This is distance to the shown exemplars, not similarity across participants.

company_involvement.description: Authors are at Kellogg School of Management. The experiments ran on freelancer.com; Study 1 exemplars came from the focal brand's 2019 private contest; training logos were acquired from a crowdsourcing design platform. No AI-company authorship or funding is stated.
company_involvement.locator: PDF p. 1; PDF p. 16 (printed p. 15); PDF p. 17 footnote 1

eligibility.reason: Study 1 randomizes 440 registered professional designers across four galleries, two of which show AI-generated logo variations (ideas_supplied), against a no-exemplar arm (Blind) and a human-exemplar arm (Open); 292 designers who submitted are analyzed (146 in the focal Variation(1) vs Blind contrast). Outcomes are scored on submitted logos (CLIP-distance originality, survey click attractiveness, perceived originality). Study 2 replicates with 208 analyzed designers. Caveat: AI enters only as pre-generated examples; designers never use a model themselves.

one_line_finding: Among professional logo designers, seeing one AI variation per exemplar raised mean click-attractiveness quality over no exemplars (0.5718 vs 0.5054, difference 0.0665, SE 0.0197; Table WA-C.3) without changing top-50 originality (difference -0.0035, SE 0.0054), and gave higher originality than seeing the original exemplars (Open minus Variation -0.0139, SE 0.0053; Table WA-C.4); the restaurant replication shows the same pattern (Tables WA-D.4, WA-D.5).
open_questions: Is a gallery of pre-generated AI images (no interaction with a model) 'generative-AI assistance' under criterion 1? It fits the ideas_supplied role, but no participant used AI directly.

Originality is the distance of each submission to the 12 top original exemplars, which the Variation arms never saw. Coded as novelty (with_ai), not as diversity across people; the paper reports no across-participant similarity measure.
Which arm is the primary AI arm for the Variation vs Blind contrast in Study 1: Variation(1) (paper's focal arm) or Variation(4)? Variation(4) vs Blind and vs Open are not printed for Study 1.
Originality is analyzed only for the top 50 submissions by quality per condition (a post-treatment selection on another outcome); the number of designers behind those 200 submissions is not stated.
Study 2 does not state explicitly that its 485 registered designers were the randomized count; n_randomized left null.
notes: PDF page = printed page + 1 in the main text; Web Appendix page WA-k = PDF page 44 + k. All standard errors are clustered by designer (submission-level regressions), so they qualify under codebook section 10; no participant-level arm SDs are printed. Table WA-C.2 (N = 200) and WA-C.1 (N = 2199) appear to include the Variation(4) arm in the regression but print no Variation(4) coefficient. Figure 9 and Figure 10 captions swap the panel descriptions relative to the panel labels. Not coded as studies: (a) the 100-person click survey used to train the Optimization LoRA and other pipeline validation surveys (WA-B.3), which score AI outputs only; (b) the refinement comparison (Figure 10), in which professionals polished AI variations and the top-50 Variation(1) submissions scored higher on originality (Delta 0.017, p < 0.001) and quality (Delta 0.295, p < 0.001) than the refined variations, a non-randomized mechanism check. Appendix E reports design-element transmission (Tables E.1-E.3), not a creativity outcome.
